hook_text: She chalked up R15. Then tried R9. By packing-up time the market row had taught her its one law.
clip_script: Saturday morning, the street market. Sixty crates of butternuts in one long row, every butternut identical. A grower joins the row and chalks up fifteen rand a kilo while everyone else asks twelve. Shoppers glance, drift one crate along, buy identical butternuts for twelve. She sells nothing. So she swings to nine rand — sells out before ten o'clock. Smart? No. The row would have taken everything she had at twelve. She just gifted three rand on every single kilo. By the time she loads the bakkie she knows the row's one law: the price is twelve because the WHOLE row made it twelve, and no single crate can move it. Economists call her a price taker, and the only decision she keeps is how many kilos to bring. Even that follows one rule: keep loading kilos while the next one earns more than it costs — stop when the next kilo would cost more than the twelve it fetches. That's the famous MR equals MC, and it's just refusing to sell at a loss, kilo by kilo. And the ending worth remembering: if butternut sellers start clearing pure profit, nothing stops crate sixty-one from arriving. More crates, more butternuts, the price eases — until every seller earns a fair return and not a cent more. Profit is the advertisement. Entry is the reply.
visual_style: A single long market row drawn in warm morning light, sixty butternut crates stretching to a vanishing point; a chalkboard price flips 15 to 9 to 12 above one crate while shoppers flow like water toward the cheapest identical pile.
mood: Street-smart and playful, sharpening into one clean economic law.
pacing: Two quick failure beats at fifteen and nine, a calm landing at twelve, then an accelerating crates-arriving montage to the closing line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to draw the whole perfect-market picture — flat line, tick, U and rectangle — from one market morning.
